read: full: main text pp. 1-11 (abstract, Secs. 1-6, limitations) read in full; appendices (pp. 14-21: PRM-guided search, supplementary best-of-N results, prompts) skimmed
venue_now: Findings of ACL 2025 per the catalogue. The text file is arXiv 2501.07301v2 (5 Jun 2025, Qwen Team) and has no venue header.
what_it_is: The Qwen team's report on building math PRMs; it releases Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B and -72B (p. 1). Its experiments find that Monte Carlo (MC) step labels give worse PRMs than LLM-as-judge or human labels, because completions can reach correct answers from incorrect steps and incorrect answers from correct ones (pp. 1-5). They also find best-of-N evaluation of PRMs biased in three ways (pp. 6-8): policies produce correct answers through flawed processes, PRMs tolerate them, and many PRMs place their minimum score on the final-answer step. The remedy is consensus filtering: MC labels are kept only where a Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct judge agrees on the error location. The released PRMs are evaluated with both best-of-8 and ProcessBench (pp. 5, 9-10).
domain: math: GSM8K, MATH, Minerva Math, GaoKao 2023 En, OlympiadBench, College Math and MMLU STEM for best-of-8, plus ProcessBench (pp. 3, 9)
size: Training: about 500,000 queries with gold answers, 6-8 responses each, 8 completions per step (p. 3). Comparison sets of 860k samples, about 40% kept after consensus filtering; separately, 3M MC samples cut to 1.5M (pp. 4-5). Evaluation: best-of-8 on 7 math benchmarks and ProcessBench's 3,400 cases (pp. 3, 9-10), with 9 other PRMs, one outcome reward model (Qwen2.5-Math-RM-72B) and 6 critic LLMs compared (Tables 6-7, p. 10).
source_of_items: existing datasets (math benchmarks and ProcessBench); training responses generated by Qwen2-Math and Qwen2.5-Math models
has_gold_traces: no: training uses gold final answers; step labels come from MC rollouts filtered by an LLM judge (pp. 3, 9)
evaluation: final answer (best-of-8 accuracy, p. 3) and step-level or process (ProcessBench earliest-error F1, pp. 3, 10); also a manual check of correct-answer responses (Figure 6, p. 7)
human_validation: No new human step labels for training. The authors hand-annotated randomly chosen correct-answer responses of Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct and found process errors in 5.1% (GSM8K), 11.9% (MATH), 27.4% (OlympiadBench) and 43.4% (Omni-MATH) of them (p. 6; Figure 6, p. 7). Annotator numbers and agreement are not reported. The PRMs are validated against ProcessBench's expert labels (Table 7, p. 10).
contamination_measures: PRM800K training data deduplicated against the test set (p. 4); otherwise none

engtrace_use.explanation: Candidate; the May paper does not cite it. EngTrace's validation reports results for the two PRMs it releases: Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-72B (step AUROC 0.825) and -7B (0.767) (state brief Sec. 3). Any sentence naming these models needs this citation. The batch description is accurate: it releases the 7B and 72B Qwen2.5-Math-PRMs, reports that MC step labels are noisy, and shows that best-of-N rewards correct answers reached through flawed steps.

suggested_wording: We evaluate Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B and -72B (Zhang et al., 2025), whose authors report that best-of-N evaluation rewards correct answers reached through flawed steps, and that even their 72B PRM locates the error in only 58.1% of ProcessBench's correct-answer, flawed-process solutions.
facts_to_cite: Releases Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B and -72B, initialised from Qwen2.5-Math-7B/72B-Instruct and trained on consensus-filtered labels (p. 1; p. 9).

MC step labels give worse PRMs than LLM-as-judge or human labels. Average ProcessBench F1: 28.9 with Math-Shepherd's MC data and 40.1 with the authors' own MC data, against 46.5 with LLM-as-judge labels and 56.5 with PRM800K human labels (Table 4, p. 5).
MC estimation mislabels steps because completions reach correct answers from incorrect steps, or incorrect answers from correct ones (abstract, p. 1; p. 2).
Consensus filtering keeps a sample only when the MC label and a Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct judge agree on the error location; about 40% of the data survives (p. 5; p. 9).

Best-of-N is a biased PRM metric: policies produce correct answers with flawed processes, PRMs tolerate them, which inflates best-of-N, and many PRMs put their minimum score on the final-answer step (abstract, p. 1; pp. 6-8).
Hand-checked correct-answer responses of Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct contained process errors in 5.1% (GSM8K) to 43.4% (Omni-MATH) of cases (Figure 6, p. 7).

On ProcessBench cases with a correct answer but an erroneous step, Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B and -72B locate the error 53.9% and 58.1% of the time; every other open PRM tested stays below 50% (Table 5, p. 7).
Average ProcessBench F1: 73.5 (7B) and 78.3 (72B), against o1-mini 87.9 and GPT-4o 61.9 (Table 7, p. 10).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: step-level evaluation of PRMs against expert labels (through ProcessBench), and the diagnosis that answer-level evaluation hides flawed processes. EngTrace's PRM results extend its Table 5 to engineering. The 72B PRM reaches step AUROC 0.825 overall, but inside correct-answer traces its precision and recall fall to 0.246 and 0.255 (state brief Sec. 3). The metrics differ (step precision and recall against Table 5's first-error accuracy), so only the direction can be compared, not the numbers. Lacks: engineering (math only); generated instances; gold intermediate values; expert annotation of its own (its step-level check rests on ProcessBench). It is a model-training report, not a benchmark.
notes: Paragraph: process supervision and judge validity, and the evaluation section wherever the PRMs are named. Naming clash: VersaPRM calls a different checkpoint 'Qwen-2.5-Math-PRM'. That model is Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct fine-tuned on PRM800K, cited to Zheng et al. 2024 (zeng2025versaprm Table 3, p. 24), and it is neither of this paper's releases. VersaPRM's comparisons therefore do not involve the PRMs EngTrace ran. The 78.3 ProcessBench F1 for the 72B model is reported here, not in the ProcessBench paper.
